text: In two thousand, Enron was America's seventh-largest company. Twelve months later, it was bankrupt.
On paper, executives Ken Lay and Jeffrey Skilling ran a fortress, even printing a sixty-four-page Code of Ethics.
Behind it, they built a shadow network of shell companies—LJM, Raptor, Chewco—to hide thirty-eight billion dollars in debt.
While Wall Street cheered, the real numbers bled. In October two thousand one, Enron admitted a six-hundred-eighteen-million-dollar loss.
Twenty thousand workers lost their jobs and pensions. Seventy-four billion dollars in market value vanished.
Every document, signature, and shell entity pointed to one place: the largest corporate fraud of its era.
